practices.name: Human-Centered Design
practices.meta_description: Human-centered design consulting that pairs field research with evidence to redesign services, experiences and workplaces around the people they serve.
practices.tagline: Services, experiences and workplaces designed with the people who use and deliver them.
intro: Our Human-Centered Design practice helps organizations redesign the services, experiences and workplaces that shape how people are treated. We work at the point where strategy becomes something a customer, patient, resident or employee actually encounters: a waiting room, an onboarding week, a benefits application, a shift handover. We study those moments in context, make the hidden operations behind them visible, and design changes that the organization can deliver and sustain, rather than concepts that stall after the workshop ends.

The people lens matters here because most experience failures are not interface problems. They are organizational problems that surface at the front line: unclear ownership, policies written without users in mind, staff who lack the tools or authority to help. When employees struggle to deliver a service, customers feel it. When customers are confused, staff absorb the friction. Designing for both sides of that relationship at once is how service quality improves and stays improved.

We pair qualitative depth with quantitative rigor. Contextual inquiry, diary studies and co-design sessions tell us why something happens; operational data, survey results and behavioral analytics tell us how often and for whom. Following our Listen, Measure, Design, Deliver, Sustain method, every recommendation is traceable to evidence, tested with the people it affects, and handed over with the measures leaders need to know whether it is working.

themes.title: Frontstage and backstage, together
themes.body: A service is only as good as the processes, systems and people behind it. We map both the visible experience and the backstage operations that produce it, so that design decisions account for staffing, policy, technology and handoffs. The result is change that front-line teams can actually deliver, not a polished journey that breaks on contact with reality.

themes.title: Evidence before ideation
themes.body: Workshops are useful, but ideas generated without research tend to reflect the assumptions already in the room. We ground design work in field research and data, distinguishing what people say from what they do, and what is common from what is merely memorable. That discipline keeps investment focused on the problems that matter most to the people affected.

themes.title: Designing with, not for
themes.body: The people closest to a problem usually understand it best. We bring customers, employees and community members into the design process as partners, with fair compensation, accessible formats and clear decision rights. Co-design improves the quality of solutions, builds the trust needed for adoption, and makes sure that people who are often excluded from design decisions shape the outcome.

practices.name: People Analytics & Data
practices.meta_description: People analytics consulting that turns workforce data into sound decisions on retention, pay equity, workforce planning and culture, with ethics built in.
practices.tagline: Rigorous, ethical people analytics that help leaders make better decisions about their workforce.
intro: Our People Analytics & Data practice helps leaders answer the questions that matter most about their workforce: who is likely to leave and why, whether pay is fair, where collaboration is breaking down, what skills the strategy will require, and whether investments in people are paying off. We build the analyses, models, data foundations and dashboards that turn scattered HR, finance and operational data into evidence that executives, boards and investors can act on with confidence.

The people lens matters because workforce data describes human beings. Analysis done carelessly can expose individuals, encode historical bias into predictions, or reduce complex experiences to a single score. We treat privacy, consent, transparency and fairness as design requirements, not afterthoughts. We aggregate responsibly, test models for disparate impact, and explain findings in language that employees and managers can understand and trust.

Our work combines statistical depth with practical judgment. We use methods suited to the question, from regression-based pay equity models and survival analysis to organizational network analysis and text analytics, and we pair quantitative findings with listening so that numbers carry their context. Using our Listen, Measure, Design, Deliver, Sustain method, we leave clients with stronger internal capability, sound governance and measures they can maintain on their own.

themes.title: Decisions, not dashboards
themes.body: Analytics earns its keep when it changes a decision. We start every engagement by defining the decisions leaders face and the evidence they would need to make them well, then work backward to the data and methods. That focus prevents the common pattern of building reports that are admired once and rarely opened again.

themes.title: Ethics by design
themes.body: People data carries obligations. We apply data minimization, minimum group sizes for reporting, role-based access and documented model governance, and we test predictive tools for fairness across demographic groups. Clear communication with employees about what is collected and why is part of the work, because trust is the precondition for honest data.

themes.title: Numbers with context
themes.body: A turnover rate or an engagement score rarely explains itself. We pair quantitative analysis with interviews, focus groups and open-text analysis so that leaders understand the mechanisms behind the metrics. This combination produces recommendations that address root causes and helps avoid confident action based on correlations that do not hold up.

services.name: Service Design
services.meta_title: Service Design Consulting: Blueprints to Delivery
services.meta_description: Service design consulting that maps frontstage and backstage operations, redesigns end-to-end services with staff and users, and supports implementation.
services.summary: End-to-end service redesign that aligns what customers experience with the people, processes and systems that deliver it behind the scenes.
services.lede: Our service design consulting aligns the experience your customers, patients or residents receive with the people, processes, policies and systems that produce it, so improvements hold up in daily operations.
challenge: Most organizations do not design their services; they accumulate them. A process built for one channel is extended to three. A policy written to manage risk adds a form, a handoff and a wait. Each department optimizes its own step, and no one owns the end-to-end experience. The result is familiar to anyone who has tried to resolve a billing error, enroll in a benefit or schedule a follow-up appointment: repeated questions, unclear status, and staff who apologize for systems they did not design and cannot change.

These failures carry real costs. Rework and failure demand, the contacts that exist only because something went wrong earlier, consume capacity that could serve people better. Front-line employees absorb customer frustration, which erodes morale and drives turnover in roles that are expensive to refill. Leaders often respond with a new app or a channel strategy, but digital fixes rarely solve backstage problems. Effective service design consulting starts by seeing the whole system, including the parts customers never see.

approach.title: Observe the service in context
approach.body: We conduct contextual inquiry with customers and staff, shadow front-line work across shifts and channels, and interview the backstage teams in operations, IT, compliance and finance whose decisions shape the experience. We pay particular attention to workarounds, which reveal where formal processes fail. This fieldwork produces a grounded picture of how the service actually runs, not how the procedure manual says it should.

approach.title: Quantify where the service breaks
approach.body: We analyze contact reasons, cycle times, handoff counts, abandonment points and repeat contacts to separate value demand from failure demand. Where possible we link operational data to satisfaction and effort measures by journey stage. This baseline shows which breakdowns affect the most people, which carry the highest cost to serve, and which disproportionately affect particular groups of customers.

approach.title: Blueprint and prototype the future service
approach.body: We build current-state and future-state service blueprints that connect customer actions, frontstage interactions, backstage processes and support systems, with the line of visibility made explicit. Working with staff and customers, we prototype new service concepts at increasing fidelity, from role-played scenarios to live pilots, and test them against both experience goals and operational constraints such as staffing, systems and regulation.

approach.title: Pilot, refine and scale
approach.body: We help teams run controlled pilots, update standard operating procedures, retrain staff and adjust system requirements. We work alongside your operations and change leads rather than handing over a deck, sequencing changes so that quick improvements build credibility while structural fixes progress. Front-line employees are involved in refinement, which improves both the design and its adoption.

approach.title: Assign ownership and measure
approach.body: We help establish journey or service ownership roles with real decision rights, and set up a small set of measures covering experience, effort, failure demand and staff experience. We document blueprints as living artifacts, train internal teams in service design methods, and define a review cadence so the service continues to improve after our engagement ends.

Failure demand and contact reason analysis
Future-state service blueprint with prioritized changes
Tested prototypes and pilot results summary
Implementation roadmap with owners and dependencies
Service performance measures and ownership model
outcomes: Customers complete key tasks with fewer handoffs, repeated questions and unexplained waits
Front-line staff have the information and authority to resolve issues the first time
Leaders can see and manage the service end to end instead of by department
Operational capacity shifts from fixing failures toward serving people well
services.who_we_serve: Chief operating officers, chief customer officers, heads of patient or member experience, and public agency directors who are accountable for a service that crosses departmental lines. We often begin when complaint volumes rise, a digital program underdelivers, a merger combines two ways of serving customers, or a regulator or board asks for evidence of fair treatment. Clients include health systems, financial institutions, government agencies, nonprofits delivering direct services, and portfolio companies preparing for growth.
services.impact_lens: Well-designed services respect people's time, dignity and circumstances. For customers and residents, that can mean fewer barriers to care, benefits or support, especially for those with less time, money or digital access to navigate complexity. For employees, it means less moral friction from enforcing processes that do not work and more capacity to help. For communities, public and mission-driven services that function well build trust in institutions, which is a social good in its own right.

faqs.q: What is the difference between service design and UX design?
faqs.a: UX design typically focuses on a digital product or interface. Service design looks at the entire service across every channel and touchpoint, including the backstage people, processes, policies and systems that make it work. A well-designed app cannot fix a service if the team behind it lacks authority to resolve issues. Service design consulting addresses both the experience and the operational system, and often informs UX work as one component.

faqs.q: What is a service blueprint?
faqs.a: A service blueprint is a diagram that shows a service from the customer's perspective alongside the frontstage interactions, backstage activities and support systems that deliver it. It separates what customers see from what they do not, using a line of visibility, and exposes handoffs, delays and failure points. Blueprints help operations, technology and experience teams agree on what is happening today and what must change to deliver a better future state.

faqs.q: How long does a service design engagement take?
faqs.a: Scope drives timing. A focused diagnostic of a single journey, including field research and a current-state blueprint, is typically a matter of weeks. A full redesign that includes prototyping, pilots and implementation support usually runs over several months. We often structure work in stages so leaders can review findings and decide on investment before committing to the next phase, and so that early improvements can begin while larger changes are planned.

faqs.q: Do you replace our internal design or CX team?
faqs.a: No. We work alongside internal design, customer experience, operations and change teams, and we aim to leave them stronger. Many clients engage us to bring research capacity, an outside perspective on cross-departmental issues, or experience with blueprinting and piloting at scale. We share methods, templates and artifacts openly and can include coaching or training so that your team can continue service design work independently.

services.name: Experience Design
services.meta_title: Experience Design Consulting for Customers & Users
services.meta_description: Experience design consulting that shapes how customers feel at the moments that matter, across physical, digital and human touchpoints, grounded in research.
services.summary: Research-led design of the moments customers and users remember, across digital, physical and human interactions, built around real needs and emotions.
services.lede: Our experience design consulting shapes how people feel and behave at the moments that matter most, across digital, physical and human touchpoints, using research to design experiences that earn trust and loyalty.
challenge: Customers rarely judge an organization by its average interaction. They remember the peaks and the endings: the call where someone finally solved the problem, the confusing letter that arrived after a loss, the first day using a new product. Yet many organizations measure experience as a single satisfaction score and invest evenly across touchpoints. Effort goes to features that are easy to build rather than moments that shape loyalty, and experiences are designed channel by channel, so the tone, information and promises customers receive do not match.

The underlying problem is often a gap in understanding. Teams rely on personas built from demographics and assumptions rather than on the needs, motivations and contexts that actually drive behavior. Emotional and cognitive load, such as anxiety during a medical decision or confusion in a financial one, goes unaddressed because it does not appear in operational data. Without that understanding, design decisions default to internal convenience, and customers experience the organization as a set of disconnected departments rather than a coherent relationship.

approach.title: Understand needs and emotions
approach.body: We use in-depth interviews, contextual observation and diary studies to understand what people are trying to accomplish, what worries them, and how they make decisions over time. We frame findings using jobs to be done, focusing on the progress people seek rather than product features. This reveals the functional, emotional and social dimensions of the experience that surveys alone cannot capture.

approach.title: Identify the moments that matter
approach.body: We combine survey data, behavioral analytics and operational records to find the moments with the greatest influence on trust, loyalty and outcomes. Driver analysis helps distinguish the interactions that shape overall perception from those that merely generate noise. We segment results by customer group so that the experiences of less-represented customers are visible rather than averaged away.

approach.title: Design experience principles and concepts
approach.body: We translate research into behavioral archetypes, experience principles and concepts for priority moments. Archetypes based on needs and mindsets tend to be more durable than demographic personas. We sketch, prototype and test concepts with real users, from conversation guides and communications to digital flows and physical environments, iterating until the experience is clear, accessible and emotionally appropriate.

approach.title: Bring the experience to life
approach.body: We work with product, marketing, operations and front-line teams to implement designs consistently across channels. That includes content and tone guidance, interaction specifications, staff scripts that allow judgment, and training on the intent behind the design. We support launch with structured testing so that teams can adjust quickly based on how real customers respond.

approach.title: Embed experience governance
approach.body: We help set experience measures tied to the priority moments, establish a cross-functional forum that reviews them, and create a design system or playbook so new touchpoints follow the same principles. Customer feedback loops are connected to teams with the authority to act, which keeps the experience coherent as products, channels and staff change over time.

Behavioral archetypes based on needs and mindsets
Moments that matter analysis with driver modeling
Experience principles and tone of voice guidance
Tested concepts and prototypes for priority moments
Experience playbook and measurement framework
outcomes: Customers experience a consistent, coherent relationship across channels and interactions
Investment concentrates on the moments that most influence trust and loyalty
Teams share a research-based understanding of customer needs and motivations
Experiences reduce anxiety and confusion at emotionally significant points in the journey
services.who_we_serve: Chief marketing, customer and digital officers, product leaders and brand leaders in organizations where trust is central to the relationship. Typical triggers include a new product or brand launch, declining loyalty or retention, a shift to digital channels that has weakened personal relationships, or a strategic move into a new customer segment. We work with financial services firms, health and benefits providers, consumer businesses, hospitality operators and mission-driven organizations that serve diverse populations.
services.impact_lens: Experience design shapes how people feel about institutions that hold significant power in their lives. Clear, respectful experiences reduce stress for customers facing difficult decisions and make services easier to use for people with limited time, literacy or digital confidence. Employees benefit when experiences are designed to support their judgment rather than script it. When an organization consistently treats people well at moments of vulnerability, it builds the kind of trust that benefits communities and sustains long-term relationships.

faqs.q: What does an experience design consultant do?
faqs.a: An experience design consultant researches how people interact with an organization, identifies the moments that most shape their perceptions and outcomes, and designs better experiences across digital, physical and human touchpoints. The work spans research, concept development, prototyping and implementation support. Good experience design consulting is grounded in evidence about real user needs rather than internal assumptions, and it considers how front-line staff and systems will deliver the experience.

faqs.q: What is the difference between personas and archetypes?
faqs.a: Personas usually describe fictional individuals with demographic details, such as age, job and family. Archetypes describe patterns of need, motivation and behavior that cut across demographics, such as someone who wants control versus someone who wants reassurance. Archetypes are often more useful for design because they reflect why people behave as they do and are less likely to reinforce stereotypes. We use whichever form best supports the decisions your teams need to make.

faqs.q: How is experience design different from service design?
faqs.a: The two overlap considerably. Experience design focuses on how an interaction feels and functions from the user's perspective, including emotion, content and interaction quality. Service design extends further into the backstage operations, roles and systems that deliver the experience. Many engagements combine both: experience design defines what good looks like at key moments, and service design ensures the organization can deliver it reliably.

faqs.q: How do you measure the value of experience design?
faqs.a: We define measures before design begins, tied to the specific moments being improved. These may include task completion, customer effort, trust and satisfaction at that stage, downstream behaviors such as retention or adherence, and operational measures such as repeat contacts. We also track staff experience where employees deliver the change. Comparing pilot and control groups, where feasible, gives leaders credible evidence of what changed.

services.name: Employee Experience Design
services.meta_description: Employee experience design consulting that researches and redesigns the moments that shape how people join, work, grow and leave, tied to retention and service.
services.summary: Redesign of the moments that shape working life, from hiring and onboarding to growth and exit, using research, data and co-design with employees.
services.lede: Our employee experience design work researches and redesigns the moments that shape how people join, work, grow and leave your organization, so that employees can do their best work and serve customers well.
challenge: Most organizations know their employee experience matters but manage it in fragments. Recruiting owns the candidate experience, HR operations owns onboarding paperwork, IT owns equipment, managers own everything else, and no one owns the whole. New hires spend their first week waiting for system access. Internal transfers feel like starting over. Policies on flexibility, leave or promotion are applied inconsistently because managers interpret them differently. Engagement surveys signal that something is wrong, but they rarely show exactly where the experience breaks down or what to change.

The consequences extend beyond HR. Early tenure turnover is often the most preventable and most costly. Friction in everyday work, such as redundant approvals or poor tools, consumes time and energy that should go to customers. In frontline-heavy organizations, the experience of employees directly shapes the experience of customers. Employee experience design addresses these problems by treating work itself as a service that the organization provides to its people, with the same rigor applied to customer experience.

approach.title: Research working life as it is
approach.body: We conduct interviews, focus groups and job shadowing across roles, locations and tenure bands, with deliberate inclusion of frontline, remote and hourly employees who are often underrepresented in corporate research. Diary studies capture experiences such as onboarding or return from leave over time. We listen for the moments that shape whether people feel capable, respected and connected to their work.

approach.title: Connect experience to outcomes
approach.body: We analyze survey results, HR system data, exit data and operational metrics together to identify where experience gaps relate to attrition, absence, time to productivity or service quality. We look at differences across demographic groups, roles and managers to find where experiences diverge. This evidence focuses design effort on moments with the strongest link to outcomes employees and leaders both care about.

approach.title: Co-design the moments that matter
approach.body: We map the employee lifecycle and blueprint priority moments such as hiring, onboarding, first promotion, becoming a manager, parental leave and exit. Employees and managers co-design improvements with us, which raises the quality of ideas and builds ownership. We prototype changes, from onboarding sequences to manager guides and policy wording, and test them with real employees before rollout.

approach.title: Coordinate across HR, IT and operations
approach.body: Employee experience improvements cross functional lines, so we help set up cross-functional teams with clear ownership for each moment. We support pilots, manager enablement, communications and changes to HR technology configuration. We sequence work to deliver visible early improvements, which builds credibility with employees who may be skeptical after previous survey cycles with little follow-through.

approach.title: Build continuous listening into the lifecycle
approach.body: We design lifecycle pulse surveys at key moments, define a small set of experience and outcome measures, and build dashboards for HR and line leaders. We help establish an employee experience governance forum and a cadence for reviewing results and acting on them, so the organization keeps improving the experience as roles, policies and workplaces change.

Employee archetypes reflecting differing needs across the workforce
Blueprints for priority moments such as onboarding
Co-designed and tested improvements with implementation plans
Lifecycle listening design and measurement framework
Employee experience governance model and ownership roles
outcomes: New hires reach confidence and productivity sooner with a coherent onboarding experience
Employees experience policies and processes as fair, consistent and easy to navigate
Leaders know which moments drive attrition and engagement and act on them

services.who_we_serve: Chief people officers, heads of employee experience, HR operations leaders and chief operating officers in organizations where people are central to the service model. Common triggers include high early attrition, engagement results that have stalled despite action plans, a return-to-office or hybrid transition, an HR technology implementation, rapid growth, or an acquisition that brings together different employee experiences. We work with health systems, retailers, hospitality groups, professional services firms, nonprofits and portfolio companies.
services.impact_lens: Work occupies a large share of people's lives, and the way it is designed affects their health, dignity and economic security. Better employee experiences reduce unnecessary stress, make growth opportunities more visible and fair, and help people feel valued. Those effects reach customers through better service and reach communities through more stable employment and healthier workers. Designing work with employees, rather than for them, also strengthens the voice of people whose perspectives are often missing from organizational decisions.

faqs.q: What is employee experience design?
faqs.a: Employee experience design applies human-centered design methods to working life. It studies how employees experience key moments, such as joining, learning, changing roles and leaving, and redesigns the policies, processes, tools and manager behaviors that shape those moments. Unlike engagement initiatives that focus on survey scores, employee experience design treats work as a service the organization provides and improves it through research, prototyping and measurement.

faqs.q: How is this different from an engagement survey program?
faqs.a: Engagement surveys measure how employees feel overall and can highlight problem areas, but they rarely explain what is causing the issue or what to change. Employee experience design starts with research into specific moments, connects experiences to outcomes like retention, and designs and tests concrete improvements. We often integrate survey programs into the work as one source of evidence and as a way to track whether changes are working.

faqs.q: Which moments should we focus on first?
faqs.a: It depends on your workforce and goals, but onboarding, the transition into management, internal mobility, leave and return, and exit are common priorities because they strongly influence retention and performance. We use your data to identify where experience gaps are most closely linked to outcomes, and we listen to employees about where friction is greatest. That combination points to the moments where improvement will matter most.

faqs.q: Can employee experience design work for frontline and hourly workforces?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is often most valuable there. Frontline employees experience scheduling, pay accuracy, equipment, training and supervisor relationships very directly, and these factors strongly affect retention and customer service. We adapt research methods to shift patterns and work settings, including on-site observation, short mobile surveys and paid participation, so that frontline voices shape the design rather than being represented by corporate assumptions.

services.name: Human-Centered Design Consulting
services.meta_title: Human-Centered Design Consulting for Complex Problems
services.meta_description: Human-centered design consulting that frames complex problems around the people affected, then researches, prototypes and tests solutions with real evidence.
services.summary: Structured, evidence-based problem solving that frames complex organizational challenges around the people affected and tests solutions before scaling them.
services.lede: Our human-centered design consulting helps leaders tackle complex, ambiguous problems by framing them around the people affected, testing assumptions with evidence, and prototyping solutions before committing significant resources.
challenge: Some of the hardest problems organizations face do not fit neatly into a single function or a standard methodology. Why do eligible families not enroll in a program designed for them? Why do new products that tested well in surveys fail to gain adoption? Why do employees resist a tool that should make their work easier? These problems involve human behavior, institutional constraints and competing interests. Conventional planning approaches tend to jump to solutions, define success internally, and discover only at launch that people do not behave as expected.

Many organizations have tried design thinking and been disappointed. A few energetic workshops produce sticky notes and enthusiasm, but little changes. The missing elements are usually rigor and follow-through: research deep enough to challenge assumptions, clear problem framing, disciplined testing, and a path from concept to operational reality. Human-centered design consulting done well brings those elements together and connects design work to the decisions, budgets and accountabilities that determine whether change actually happens.

approach.title: Frame the problem with the people affected
approach.body: We begin by testing the problem statement itself. Through stakeholder interviews, field research and listening sessions with the people most affected, we examine whether leaders are solving the right problem. We map the system around it, including incentives, policies and power dynamics. The output is a reframed challenge and a set of explicit assumptions that need to be tested.

approach.title: Test assumptions against evidence
approach.body: We gather quantitative evidence to size the problem, identify who is most affected, and test the assumptions surfaced in research. That may involve administrative data, funnel analysis, surveys or small experiments. We rank assumptions by how critical and how uncertain they are, so that design and testing effort goes first to the beliefs that would most change the strategy if they turned out to be wrong.

approach.title: Generate and prototype options
approach.body: We run structured ideation with diverse participants, then build rough prototypes quickly to test the riskiest assumptions. Prototypes might be a service script, a mock policy, a paper form, a landing page or a role-played interaction. We test desirability, feasibility and viability together, and we make decisions to continue, pivot or stop based on what we learn, not on attachment to an idea.

approach.title: Move from prototype to pilot
approach.body: Promising concepts move into real-world pilots with defined success measures, operational owners and a learning plan. We help teams address the practical work of implementation: budgets, procurement, staffing, legal review and training. We document what is learned so that scaling decisions are based on evidence, and we help leaders communicate the rationale to the people affected.

approach.title: Build design capability
approach.body: We help clients build lasting human-centered design capability through coaching, method guides, and governance that makes room for testing and learning within existing planning and funding processes. We help define when design approaches are appropriate, how to staff them, and how to measure their contribution, so that the practice becomes part of how the organization works rather than a one-time project.

We are often engaged when an initiative has failed to gain traction, when a new program or offering must be designed for an unfamiliar population, when a funder requires evidence of community input, or when leaders want to build internal design capability. services.impact_lens: Human-centered design shifts power toward the people a decision affects by making their needs, experiences and ideas central to the process. That reduces the risk of well-intentioned programs that miss the mark and waste resources meant for public or social benefit. Employees gain a more meaningful role in solving problems rather than simply implementing solutions handed down. When applied with attention to equity, the approach helps institutions design for people at the margins, which often improves outcomes for everyone.

faqs.q: What is human-centered design?
faqs.a: Human-centered design is an approach to problem solving that starts with the needs, behaviors and contexts of the people affected. It combines qualitative research, problem framing, ideation, prototyping and testing, repeating these steps until a solution works in practice. It is often associated with product design, but it applies equally to services, policies, programs and organizational change. Its core discipline is testing assumptions with real people before scaling.

faqs.q: Is human-centered design the same as design thinking?
faqs.a: They are closely related. Design thinking usually refers to a structured process and set of mindsets popularized through innovation workshops. Human-centered design is the broader discipline, emphasizing deep research with users and continuous testing. In practice, design thinking workshops can be one tool within a human-centered design engagement. The difference that matters is rigor: research depth, clear framing, honest testing and follow-through to implementation.

faqs.q: How does human-centered design consulting fit with data and analytics?
faqs.a: They complement each other. Qualitative research reveals why people behave as they do and surfaces needs that data cannot see. Quantitative analysis shows how widespread a problem is, who is most affected, and whether a change is working. We combine both throughout the process, using data to size and test what research uncovers and using research to interpret what the numbers show.

faqs.q: When is human-centered design not the right approach?
faqs.a: It is less suited to problems with a known solution that simply needs execution, or to decisions where there is no meaningful flexibility in what can change. It also requires leaders willing to act on what they learn, including evidence that challenges existing plans. We are candid in early conversations about whether a design approach fits your situation and will recommend alternatives when they are more appropriate.

services.name: Design Research
services.meta_title: Design Research Services: Field & User Research
services.meta_description: Design research services using contextual inquiry, diary studies and mixed methods to learn what people need so teams build products and services that work.
services.summary: Rigorous qualitative and mixed-methods research, from contextual inquiry to diary studies, that shows how people actually live, work and make decisions.
services.lede: Our design research services use contextual inquiry, diary studies, interviews and mixed methods to show how people actually behave and decide, giving your teams evidence they can design and invest against with confidence.
challenge: Organizations make consequential decisions about products, services and programs with a surprisingly thin understanding of the people they serve. Customer knowledge often lives in survey scores, sales anecdotes and the opinions of whoever spoke last in the meeting. Surveys capture what people say in response to the questions asked, not what they do or what they would never think to mention. Focus groups favor confident voices. Analytics show behavior without explaining it. The result is design that reflects internal assumptions, and expensive surprises after launch.

When organizations do commission research, it often fails to influence decisions. Studies are scoped too broadly or too late, findings arrive as long reports that are hard to act on, and samples miss the people whose needs differ most from the mainstream. Research becomes a box to check rather than an input to strategy. Effective design research services are scoped around real decisions, use methods matched to the question, include people at the margins, and translate findings into clear implications for design.

approach.title: Scope research around decisions
approach.body: We start by clarifying what decisions the research must inform and what leaders already believe. We review existing data and studies, interview internal stakeholders, and write explicit research questions and hypotheses. This prevents research that confirms what is already known and focuses fieldwork on genuine uncertainty. We also agree on how findings will be used and by whom.

approach.title: Design a sound sample and method mix
approach.body: We select methods to fit the question: contextual inquiry and observation for workflows, diary studies for experiences that unfold over time, in-depth interviews for decision-making, card sorts and tree tests for information architecture, and surveys to size patterns. We design purposive samples that include edge cases and underrepresented groups, and we document recruitment criteria so findings can be interpreted honestly.

approach.title: Conduct fieldwork and synthesize rigorously
approach.body: Our researchers conduct fieldwork in homes, workplaces, clinics, branches and community settings, with informed consent and fair compensation. We synthesize through structured coding and affinity analysis, distinguishing patterns from individual anecdotes and noting how confident we are in each finding. Outputs include insight statements, mental models, archetypes and journey frameworks that translate directly into design opportunities.

approach.title: Turn insight into action
approach.body: We present findings in working sessions rather than lengthy reports, helping product, service and leadership teams translate insights into design principles, opportunity areas and priorities. We share video clips and quotes, with consent, to make participants' experiences tangible. Where useful, we move directly into concept testing so that research insights are validated against early solutions.

approach.title: Build a research repository and practice
approach.body: We help organizations create a searchable research repository so insights accumulate rather than disappear. We set up research operations basics: consent templates, participant panels, data retention rules and ethical review steps. We also train internal teams in interviewing and synthesis so they can run lighter-weight studies on their own and know when to call for deeper work.

faqs.q: What is design research?
faqs.a: Design research is the study of people's needs, behaviors, contexts and motivations in order to inform the design of products, services, programs and policies. It relies mainly on qualitative methods such as contextual inquiry, interviews, observation and diary studies, often combined with surveys or analytics. Unlike market research, which often measures preferences and attitudes, design research focuses on understanding behavior deeply enough to design something that works.

faqs.q: What is contextual inquiry?
faqs.a: Contextual inquiry is a research method in which a researcher observes and talks with people while they perform real tasks in their own environment, such as a nurse charting at a workstation or a small business owner doing payroll. It reveals workarounds, interruptions, tools and tacit knowledge that people rarely mention in interviews. It is especially valuable for understanding complex workflows and designing services or tools that fit real conditions.

faqs.q: When should we use a diary study?
faqs.a: Diary studies are useful when the experience you want to understand unfolds over days or weeks, such as onboarding to a new job, managing a chronic condition, or using a product in daily life. Participants record experiences as they happen through short entries, photos or voice notes, which reduces recall bias. Diary studies are often paired with interviews at the start and end to explore patterns in depth.

faqs.q: How many participants do you need for qualitative research?
faqs.a: There is no single number. Qualitative research aims for depth and saturation, the point where new interviews add few new themes, rather than statistical representativeness. The right sample depends on how varied the population and experiences are. We typically design samples around meaningful segments and edge cases, and we pair qualitative work with surveys or data analysis when leaders need to know how widespread a pattern is.

services.name: Customer & Employee Journey Mapping
services.meta_description: Customer journey mapping and employee journey mapping built on research and data, showing where experiences break down and what to fix first, with clear owners.
services.summary: Evidence-based customer and employee journey maps that show where experiences break down, why it happens, and which improvements will matter most.
services.lede: Our customer journey mapping and employee journey mapping services combine field research with operational data to show where experiences break down, why they break, and which fixes will matter most to people and performance.
challenge: Journey maps have become common, and many organizations have several on the wall. Too often they were built in a single workshop from internal opinion, describe an idealized path that few customers actually follow, and stop at the edge of the customer experience without connecting to the operations behind it. They look polished but do not answer the questions leaders care about: where are we losing people, which pain points matter most, who owns the fix, and how will we know if it worked?

Employee journeys receive even less rigor. Hiring, onboarding, internal mobility and exit are typically designed by separate teams and rarely viewed from the employee's perspective as a single experience. Yet the employee journey and the customer journey are connected: a frontline worker who cannot get answers from internal systems cannot give answers to customers. Useful customer journey mapping links both perspectives, is built on evidence, quantifies impact, and connects to the people and processes responsible for change.

approach.title: Gather journey evidence from real people
approach.body: We interview and observe customers and employees across segments, channels and outcomes, including people who abandoned the journey, not only those who completed it. We capture actions, thoughts, emotions and touchpoints at each stage, and we talk with frontline staff who see where journeys go wrong every day. This grounds the map in lived experience rather than assumed paths.

approach.title: Quantify drop-off and pain points
approach.body: We connect journey stages to data: funnel conversion, time between stages, contact reasons, complaint themes, survey scores and attrition. We look at variation across segments to identify where particular groups struggle more. Quantification turns a descriptive map into a decision tool, showing which pain points affect the most people and which are most strongly linked to outcomes leaders track.

approach.title: Build maps that connect to operations
approach.body: We create current-state maps for each priority journey, layering customer or employee experience over the touchpoints, teams and systems involved. Where useful we extend maps into service blueprints. We facilitate working sessions with journey owners to identify root causes and design future-state journeys, prioritizing opportunities by impact on people, effort to deliver and strategic fit.

approach.title: Translate maps into a change portfolio
approach.body: We turn journey opportunities into a prioritized portfolio of initiatives with owners, scope and measures. We help teams test priority fixes quickly and sequence larger changes within existing planning cycles. Maps are designed to be shared widely, giving executives, frontline teams and technology partners a common reference for why each change matters and who it serves.

approach.title: Manage journeys as living assets
approach.body: We help assign journey owners, define journey-level measures, and set a regular review rhythm. Maps are kept in editable formats and updated as new research and data arrive. We often connect journey stages to dashboards so leaders can track experience and outcomes by stage, and we train teams to maintain and extend the maps without outside support.

Journey analytics showing drop-off, effort and segment differences

services.impact_lens: Journey mapping makes visible the burden that organizations quietly place on people: the forms, waits, repeated explanations and uncertainty. Seeing journeys from the perspective of the person living them helps organizations remove barriers that fall hardest on those with the least time, money or support. Mapping employee and customer journeys together recognizes that staff wellbeing and service quality are linked. For mission-driven organizations, journey maps often reveal where eligible people fall out of programs designed to help them.

faqs.q: What is customer journey mapping?
faqs.a: Customer journey mapping is a method for visualizing the steps, interactions, thoughts and emotions a customer goes through to achieve a goal with an organization, such as opening an account or resolving a problem. A good journey map is based on research rather than assumptions, highlights pain points and moments that matter, and connects the customer experience to the teams and systems responsible. It helps leaders prioritize improvements and align functions around the customer.

faqs.q: What is an employee journey map?
faqs.a: An employee journey map applies the same method to the experience of working in an organization, covering stages such as recruitment, onboarding, development, internal moves and exit. It shows how employees experience processes owned by different functions, where friction and disengagement occur, and how experiences differ across roles and groups. Employee journey maps help HR and operations leaders design a more coherent, fair and supportive experience of work.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a journey map and a service blueprint?
faqs.a: A journey map focuses on the experience from the customer or employee perspective, including actions, emotions and touchpoints. A service blueprint extends below the surface to show the frontstage staff interactions, backstage processes and support systems that produce that experience. Journey maps are useful for prioritizing what to improve. Blueprints are useful for understanding how to change the operations that deliver it.

faqs.q: How many journeys should we map?
faqs.a: Fewer than most organizations expect. We usually recommend starting with a small number of high-priority journeys tied to strategic goals, such as onboarding new customers or retaining early-tenure employees, and mapping them in depth with research and data. A broad catalog of shallow maps is less useful than a few rigorous ones with clear owners and measures. Additional journeys can follow once the approach is established.

services.name: Design Thinking Workshops
services.meta_title: Design Thinking Workshops & Facilitation for Teams
services.meta_description: Design thinking workshops that pair expert facilitation with real research and follow-through, helping leadership teams frame problems and test ideas quickly.
services.summary: Facilitated workshops grounded in real research that help leadership and cross-functional teams frame problems, generate options and test ideas with users.
services.lede: Our design thinking workshops give leadership and cross-functional teams a structured, evidence-based way to frame problems, generate options and test ideas with real users, with follow-through so the work continues after the session.
challenge: Design thinking workshops have a mixed reputation, and for good reason. Many follow a generic script: empathize, define, ideate, prototype, test, compressed into a single day with no real users in the room. Participants enjoy the energy, wall space fills with sticky notes, and then everyone returns to their normal work. Ideas are rarely tested, ownership is unclear, and the organization concludes that design thinking does not work. Meanwhile the original problem, often a stubborn cross-functional challenge, remains unsolved.

The problem is not the method but how it is used. A workshop is a tool for a specific purpose: aligning a leadership team on a problem definition, generating options from diverse perspectives, or making rapid decisions about what to test. It works when it is grounded in research, includes the right people with real decision authority, is designed around a clear outcome, and is connected to a plan for testing and implementation. Well-run design thinking workshops accelerate decisions that would otherwise take months of meetings.

approach.title: Prepare with research and stakeholder input
approach.body: Before any session, we interview sponsors and participants to understand the problem, the politics and the decisions that need to be made. Where time allows, we conduct short research with customers, employees or community members, and bring their voices into the room through stories, quotes and video. Participants arrive with shared context rather than starting from assumptions.

approach.title: Ground the session in data
approach.body: We assemble a concise fact base: relevant performance data, journey analytics, survey results and research findings. Presenting evidence early helps groups separate facts from beliefs and focus on the most consequential issues. We also define how the workshop's success will be judged, such as decisions made, hypotheses agreed for testing, or prototypes ready for users.

approach.title: Facilitate with purpose
approach.body: We design each workshop around its objective rather than a template, selecting exercises such as how-might-we framing, assumption mapping, crazy eights, storyboarding and concept scoring. Where possible, real users join to react to early prototypes during the session. Skilled facilitation ensures quieter voices are heard, senior voices do not dominate, and disagreements are surfaced productively rather than avoided.

approach.title: Turn outputs into tested next steps
approach.body: Every workshop ends with named owners, agreed experiments and a timeline. Within days we deliver a synthesis that captures decisions, rationale and next steps, not just photos of sticky notes. We can support teams through the testing that follows, running quick user tests on prototypes and reconvening the group to decide what to pursue, change or stop.

approach.title: Build internal facilitation capability
approach.body: For organizations that want to make this a regular practice, we train internal facilitators, provide workshop guides and exercise libraries, and coach leaders on sponsoring design work effectively. We help define when a workshop is the right tool and when deeper research or analysis is needed, so the method is used where it adds the most value.

faqs.q: What happens in a design thinking workshop?
faqs.a: A design thinking workshop brings a cross-functional group together to work through a problem using structured exercises. Typical activities include reviewing research about users, reframing the problem, mapping assumptions, generating ideas, sketching concepts and prototyping. The exact agenda depends on the objective. Our design thinking workshops are tailored to the decisions your team needs to make and end with clear next steps and owners.

faqs.q: How long should a design thinking workshop be?
faqs.a: Length depends on the goal. A half-day session can align a team on a problem statement or prioritize opportunities. One to two days allows for ideation and rough prototyping. A sprint over several days can take a concept through user testing. For complex problems we often recommend a series of shorter sessions with research and testing in between, rather than a single long event.

faqs.q: Can design thinking workshops be run virtually?
faqs.a: Yes. Virtual workshops work well with careful design: shorter sessions, collaborative whiteboard tools, structured breakout groups and clear facilitation. They make it easier to include participants across locations, including frontline staff and users who could not travel. Some activities, such as physical prototyping, are better in person. We help you choose the right format based on participants, goals and constraints.

faqs.q: Do participants need prior design experience?
faqs.a: No. We design workshops for people with no design background, and many of the most valuable contributions come from participants who know the problem well but have never used these methods. We explain each exercise, model how to do it, and support participants throughout. Leaders do need to commit to acting on what the group produces, which is the most important ingredient for a workshop that leads to real change.

services.name: Community Co-Design
services.meta_description: Community co-design that brings residents, clients and stakeholders into designing programs, services and spaces as fairly compensated partners with real say.
services.summary: Participatory design that brings residents, clients and community stakeholders in as compensated partners who shape programs, services and places that affect them.
services.lede: Our community co-design work brings residents, clients and local stakeholders into the design of programs, services and places as compensated partners with real influence, producing solutions that fit community needs and earn lasting trust.
challenge: Institutions that serve communities, from public agencies and health systems to foundations, developers and employers, increasingly recognize that decisions made without community input often fail. Programs go underused, new facilities sit in the wrong place, and well-funded initiatives provoke opposition. Many respond with consultation: a public meeting, a survey, a comment period. But consultation typically asks people to react to decisions already largely made, reaches those with the most time and confidence to participate, and leaves communities feeling heard but not influential.

Genuine co-design is harder. It requires sharing power over decisions, compensating people for their time and expertise, working in accessible languages and locations, and being honest about constraints. It also requires institutions to handle disagreement and to be accountable for what they do with community input. Without those elements, participatory processes can deepen mistrust, especially in communities with long histories of extractive research or broken promises. Effective community co-design treats community members as partners and builds the relationships needed to sustain that partnership.

approach.title: Build relationships before projects
approach.body: We start by understanding the community's history with the institution and the issue, including past engagement and its outcomes. We work with trusted local organizations and community connectors to listen through conversations, gatherings and visits in familiar settings. We clarify what is genuinely open for community influence and what is fixed, so that participation is honest from the start.

approach.title: Understand the community with data
approach.body: We assemble relevant data on demographics, needs, service use and outcomes, and share it with community partners in accessible formats so they can interpret it too. Community members often identify gaps in official data and add knowledge it cannot capture. This shared fact base helps groups focus on root causes and ensures the experiences of smaller or less-visible groups are considered.

approach.title: Co-design with a representative group
approach.body: We convene a co-design group that reflects the community affected, with compensation, childcare, interpretation, accessible venues and flexible times. Using participatory methods such as community mapping, storytelling, scenario testing and prototyping, members work alongside institutional staff to generate and refine options. Decision rights are explicit, and the group shapes recommendations rather than simply commenting on them.

approach.title: Implement with community oversight
approach.body: We help institutions translate co-designed recommendations into plans, budgets and operational changes, and we support community members in reviewing implementation. Where recommendations cannot be adopted, we help leaders explain why. We test changes through pilots with community feedback, so adjustments are made before full rollout and community partners can see their influence.

approach.title: Close the loop and keep partnership going
approach.body: We report back to the wider community on what was heard, what changed and what did not. We help institutions establish standing mechanisms, such as community advisory boards with real authority, compensated feedback panels or participatory budgeting, and measures of community trust and outcomes. These structures keep community voice in decisions beyond a single project.

Clients engage us when designing new programs or facilities, responding to community opposition or distrust, fulfilling funder or regulatory requirements for meaningful engagement, preparing community benefit agreements, or shifting toward participatory grantmaking. services.impact_lens: Community co-design is a direct expression of social good: it gives people affected by decisions a meaningful role in making them. Compensating participants recognizes their expertise and removes a barrier for people who cannot afford to volunteer time. Institutions gain solutions that work better and relationships that make future work easier. Employees who participate alongside community members often gain a deeper understanding of the people they serve, which improves everyday service long after a project ends.

faqs.q: What is community co-design?
faqs.a: Community co-design is a participatory approach in which community members work alongside institutions as partners to design programs, services, policies or places that affect them. Unlike consultation, which asks people to react to proposals, co-design involves community members in defining the problem, generating options and shaping decisions. It requires shared decision rights, fair compensation, accessible processes and accountability for what happens with community input.

faqs.q: How is co-design different from community engagement?
faqs.a: Community engagement is a broad term covering many activities, from information sharing and surveys to deep partnership. Co-design sits toward the shared-power end of that range. Participants are not only asked for opinions, they help make decisions and develop solutions. Many institutions benefit from both: broad engagement to hear from many people and co-design with a smaller representative group to shape specific recommendations.

faqs.q: Should community members be paid to participate?
faqs.a: We recommend it. Community members contribute expertise about their own lives and neighborhoods, and their time has value. Compensation also makes participation possible for people who cannot afford to volunteer, which improves representation. We help clients set fair rates, choose payment methods that do not create problems for people receiving public benefits, and cover practical costs such as childcare, transportation and meals.

faqs.q: What if the community wants something we cannot deliver?
faqs.a: That is why we define constraints and decision rights at the start. Being clear about what is fixed, such as budget limits or legal requirements, and what is open helps keep co-design honest. When a community recommendation cannot be adopted, leaders should explain why and what alternatives are possible. Transparent disagreement builds more trust than vague promises, and it often leads to creative solutions within real constraints.

services.name: Inclusive & Accessible Design
services.meta_description: Inclusive and accessible design consulting covering WCAG conformance, assistive technology testing and inclusive service design for people with disabilities.
services.summary: Accessibility and inclusive design across digital, physical and service experiences, from WCAG conformance to research with disabled and underserved users.
services.lede: Our inclusive and accessible design consulting helps organizations meet WCAG and legal obligations while designing services, products and workplaces that work for people with disabilities, older adults and others too often designed out.
challenge: Accessibility is often treated as a late-stage compliance check. A product or service is designed, built and launched, then audited against WCAG success criteria and patched where it fails. That approach is expensive, leaves gaps, and misses barriers that automated tools cannot detect, such as confusing content, inaccessible phone trees, forms that time out, or in-person processes that assume everyone can stand in line, read small print or hear announcements. Legal risk is real, and so is the quieter cost of customers and employees who simply give up.

Inclusion extends beyond disability. Language, literacy, age, digital access, caregiving responsibilities, neurodivergence and cultural context all shape whether people can use a service. Organizations often design for a default user who looks like their design team, then wonder why uptake is low among the people they most want to reach. Effective accessible design consulting addresses both: rigorous conformance with recognized standards, and design practices that include people with diverse needs from the beginning.

approach.title: Research with people who face barriers
approach.body: We conduct research with people with disabilities, including users of screen readers, magnification, voice control and switch access, as well as older adults, people with limited literacy or English proficiency, and others who often face exclusion. We observe real use of products, services and spaces, and we interview employees with disabilities about workplace tools and processes. Participants are compensated and sessions are accessible.

approach.title: Audit against standards and outcomes
approach.body: We audit digital properties against WCAG 2.2 at the conformance level you require, combining automated scanning with manual expert review and assistive technology testing. We assess documents, communications, physical environments and service processes, and review relevant legal obligations with your counsel. We also look at data on usage, completion and complaints to see where exclusion shows up in outcomes.

approach.title: Design inclusively from the start
approach.body: We remediate priority barriers and redesign experiences using inclusive design principles: solve for one, extend to many; offer multiple ways to complete a task; use plain language. We co-design with people who have lived experience of exclusion, update design systems with accessible components and patterns, and test prototypes with assistive technology users before release.

approach.title: Embed accessibility in delivery
approach.body: We build accessibility into product and service development: acceptance criteria, testing in delivery pipelines, procurement requirements for vendors, and content guidelines. We train designers, developers, content writers and frontline staff on their specific responsibilities, including how to support customers with disability-related needs, and we help prioritize remediation backlogs by user impact and legal exposure.

approach.title: Govern accessibility as a program
approach.body: We help establish an accessibility policy, roles and an operating model, with a maturity roadmap, recurring audits and monitoring. We support accessibility statements and feedback mechanisms that let users report barriers and receive timely responses. Regular reporting to leadership covers conformance, remediation progress and user feedback, so accessibility becomes ongoing practice rather than a periodic project.

faqs.q: What is WCAG and which level should we meet?
faqs.a: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines are the internationally recognized standard for digital accessibility, published by the World Wide Web Consortium. They are organized into conformance levels A, AA and AAA. Level AA is the most commonly referenced target in laws, regulations and procurement requirements. We recommend confirming your specific obligations with legal counsel, and we typically audit against WCAG 2.2 AA while addressing additional barriers users identify.

faqs.q: Are automated accessibility tools enough?
faqs.a: No. Automated tools are useful for catching certain issues quickly, such as missing alternative text or color contrast failures, but they detect only a portion of WCAG issues. Many barriers, including logical focus order, meaningful link text, understandable error messages and usable screen reader flows, require manual expert review and testing with assistive technologies. Testing with disabled users adds another layer by revealing real-world usability problems.

faqs.q: What is the difference between accessible design and inclusive design?
faqs.a: Accessible design focuses on removing barriers for people with disabilities and is often measured against standards such as WCAG. Inclusive design is broader, considering the full range of human diversity, including language, age, culture, literacy, income and circumstance, and involving excluded people in the design process. Our accessible design consulting addresses both: meeting standards reliably and designing experiences that work for a wider range of people from the start.

faqs.q: Does accessibility apply to services and workplaces, not just websites?
faqs.a: Yes. Accessibility applies to every way people interact with an organization: phone systems, documents, physical locations, customer service interactions, hiring processes and workplace tools. A conformant website does not help if the follow-up letter is unreadable or the in-person appointment is inaccessible. We look at the full service and employee experience, including reasonable accommodations processes, so that accessibility holds across channels.

services.name: People Analytics

services.lede: Our people analytics consulting connects HR, finance and operational data to answer the workforce questions executives and boards care about, and builds the internal capability to keep answering them responsibly.

We also recommend clear communication with employees about how their data is used.

services.name: Strategic Workforce Planning
services.meta_description: Strategic workforce planning consulting that models future skills, capacity and cost under realistic scenarios, then builds the plans to close the gaps.
services.summary: Scenario-based planning for the skills, capacity and cost your strategy requires, with practical build, buy, borrow and redeploy plans to close the gaps.
services.lede: Our strategic workforce planning helps leaders model the skills, capacity and workforce costs their strategy will require under realistic scenarios, then build practical plans to close the gaps in ways that are fair to employees.
challenge: Strategies are usually built around markets, products and capital, while workforce implications are worked out later through annual headcount budgets. That approach treats people as a cost line rather than a capability, and it struggles with the questions that determine whether a strategy can be executed. Do we have the skills to enter this market? What happens to our frontline workforce as automation and AI change the work? Where will retirements leave critical knowledge gaps? Which roles will be hardest to fill, and how long will it take?

Many workforce planning efforts stall because they try to model everything. Large spreadsheets forecast every role in detail, take months to build, and are outdated when finished. Others never move beyond headcount to skills. Meanwhile, decisions about hiring, restructuring and reskilling are made reactively, with real costs to employees who are surprised by changes they could have prepared for. Effective strategic workforce planning focuses on the roles and skills that matter most to the strategy and on decisions that leaders can act on now.

approach.title: Connect workforce to strategy
approach.body: We interview executives and business unit leaders to understand strategic priorities, expected changes in demand, operating model shifts and technology plans. We identify critical roles and skills: those with the greatest impact on strategy and the longest lead time to develop. Conversations with frontline managers and employees reveal how work is actually changing on the ground.

approach.title: Baseline supply and model demand
approach.body: We build a baseline of current workforce supply by role, skill, location, tenure and cost, and project it forward using attrition, retirement and internal movement patterns. We model future demand under several scenarios tied to business drivers, such as volume, productivity, automation and new market entry. The gap between supply and demand shows where action is needed and when.

approach.title: Design build, buy, borrow and redeploy options
approach.body: For each critical gap we evaluate options: developing internal talent, external hiring, contingent or partner arrangements, redeploying people from declining roles, or redesigning work. We assess options for cost, speed, risk and effect on employees and communities. The result is a workforce plan with clear choices, investments and timing that leaders can debate and approve.

approach.title: Put the plan into motion
approach.body: We help translate plans into recruiting strategies, reskilling pathways, internal mobility programs, location decisions and budget changes. Where roles will decline, we support transparent planning that gives employees time and options. We work with HR, finance and business leaders to integrate workforce planning into annual planning and budgeting rather than treating it as a separate exercise.

approach.title: Make planning a recurring discipline
approach.body: We set up a lightweight, repeatable planning process with a scenario model your team can update, a small set of indicators to monitor, and triggers that prompt plan revisions. We help define roles and governance across HR, finance and the business, and train internal teams to maintain the model and lead future planning cycles.

Workforce supply baseline and forward projection

faqs.q: What is strategic workforce planning?
faqs.a: Strategic workforce planning is the process of determining the workforce an organization will need to execute its strategy, comparing that to the workforce it is likely to have, and deciding how to close the gap. It looks beyond annual headcount budgets to critical skills, multi-year time horizons and alternative scenarios. The output is a set of decisions about hiring, development, redeployment, partnerships and work design.

faqs.q: How is strategic workforce planning different from headcount planning?
faqs.a: Headcount planning sets the number of positions and associated costs for the next budget year, usually by department. Strategic workforce planning covers a longer horizon, focuses on skills and critical roles rather than position counts, and tests multiple scenarios. It informs headcount budgets but also addresses questions they cannot, such as how automation will change roles or where future skill shortages will appear.

faqs.q: How far ahead should we plan?
faqs.a: Most organizations benefit from a planning horizon of three to five years for critical roles and skills, with more detail for the near term and broader scenarios further out. The right horizon depends on how long it takes to develop key capabilities. Roles that require years of training or licensure need longer horizons. We revisit plans at least annually and when significant changes occur.

faqs.q: How do you account for AI and automation?
faqs.a: We analyze roles at the task level to estimate which activities are likely to be automated, augmented or unchanged, and how quickly, given your technology plans. We model the resulting changes in capacity and skill needs under several adoption scenarios. Just as important, we plan for how affected employees can move into new or redesigned roles, and we involve workers in redesigning work where possible.

services.name: Organizational Network Analysis
services.meta_description: Organizational network analysis consulting that maps how work and information really flow, identifies hidden influencers and bottlenecks, and guides change.
services.summary: Mapping how collaboration, information and influence actually flow across your organization, revealing hidden connectors, overloaded people and silos that charts miss.
services.lede: Our organizational network analysis maps how collaboration, information and influence actually move across your organization, revealing the connectors, bottlenecks and silos that formal org charts hide, so leaders can design and change with precision.
challenge: Org charts show reporting lines, but most work happens through informal networks: the colleague people ask for advice, the analyst who connects two departments, the manager everyone copies on decisions. Leaders redesign structures, launch change programs and integrate acquisitions without seeing these networks, and they are often surprised when change stalls, key knowledge walks out the door with a departing employee, or a new structure creates bottlenecks no one anticipated. Hybrid and remote work has made these networks both more important and harder to observe.

Collaboration also has costs. A small number of people often carry a disproportionate share of requests, meetings and decisions, which leads to burnout and slows the organization. Silos between functions or locations persist despite repeated calls for collaboration. Newer employees and some demographic groups may be less connected to the networks where opportunities and information flow. Organizational network analysis makes these patterns visible and measurable, providing evidence for decisions about structure, roles, change leadership and inclusion that otherwise rely on intuition.

approach.title: Define the questions and build trust
approach.body: We work with leaders to define what the analysis should inform, such as a reorganization, merger integration, change program or inclusion goal. We engage employee representatives and communicate openly about purpose, data use and confidentiality, because network data is sensitive. Interviews with a sample of employees help us design relevant survey questions and interpret results later.

approach.title: Collect and analyze network data
approach.body: We gather relational data through short network surveys, such as who people go to for information, advice or decisions, and where appropriate through aggregated, privacy-protected collaboration metadata. We calculate measures including degree, betweenness and eigenvector centrality, network density, brokerage and cross-group ties. We identify central connectors, overloaded individuals, isolated groups and structural holes.

approach.title: Interpret patterns and design interventions
approach.body: We interpret results with leaders and, where appropriate, with the people in the network. Findings inform specific interventions: adjusting structure to reduce bottlenecks, redistributing collaborative load, building bridges between siloed teams, designing onboarding to connect new hires faster, or enlisting informal influencers as change champions. We test proposed changes against the network to anticipate effects.

approach.title: Support targeted change
approach.body: We help implement interventions, from role redesign and meeting practices to change networks and mentoring programs. For reorganizations and integrations we help protect critical relationships during transition. We coach managers on supporting overloaded connectors and including peripheral team members, and work with HR to address retention risks among people who hold the network together.

approach.title: Track network health over time
approach.body: We design follow-up network measurements to evaluate whether interventions changed collaboration patterns as intended. We help establish governance for ongoing use of network data, including clear limits on individual-level use in performance decisions, and we build internal capability to run and interpret future analyses responsibly.
