faqs.q: What is organizational network analysis?
faqs.a: Organizational network analysis is a method for mapping and measuring the relationships through which work, information and influence flow in an organization. Data typically comes from short surveys asking who people collaborate with or seek advice from, sometimes supplemented by aggregated collaboration metadata. Network measures reveal central connectors, bottlenecks, silos and isolated individuals, informing decisions about structure, change, collaboration and inclusion.

faqs.q: What do centrality measures tell us?
faqs.a: Centrality measures describe a person's or group's position in a network. Degree centrality counts direct connections. Betweenness centrality shows how often someone sits on the paths between others, indicating brokers and potential bottlenecks. Eigenvector centrality reflects connection to other well-connected people, a signal of influence. Each measure answers a different question, so we select and interpret them based on the decisions the analysis is meant to inform.

faqs.q: Is organizational network analysis invasive?
faqs.a: It can be if designed poorly. We minimize data collection, communicate transparently with employees about purpose and use, and agree in advance on governance, including limiting individual-level results to purposes such as development and support rather than performance ratings. When using collaboration metadata, we analyze patterns in aggregate and never read message content. Done this way, ONA respects privacy while producing useful insight.

faqs.q: How is ONA used in mergers and reorganizations?
faqs.a: Before a merger or reorganization, ONA identifies critical relationships, knowledge holders and informal leaders who should be retained and engaged. It shows which teams depend on each other so new structures do not sever important connections. During integration, follow-up analysis tracks whether the combined organization is forming cross-legacy ties. This evidence helps leaders reduce disruption and preserve the capabilities the deal was meant to capture.

services.name: Employee Listening & Surveys
services.meta_description: Employee listening strategy and survey consulting: valid instruments, lifecycle pulses, open-text analysis and action planning employees can see.

challenge: Many organizations run an annual engagement survey that has become a ritual. Questions were licensed or inherited years ago, results arrive weeks later as a heat map, managers are asked to build action plans with little support, and employees see little change. Participation declines and comments grow more cynical. Leaders know something is wrong but cannot tell whether a score movement reflects real change or noise. The survey measures sentiment without explaining it, and it rarely connects to the outcomes leaders care about, like retention, safety or customer service.

Adding more surveys does not solve the problem. Pulse fatigue sets in when employees are asked frequently but see no response. Important voices are missed: frontline and hourly workers without email, people who fear being identified, and groups too small for standard reporting. Meanwhile, rich signals in exit interviews, open-text comments and frontline feedback go unanalyzed. An effective employee listening strategy is designed around decisions, uses the right method for each question, protects confidentiality, and is judged by whether employees experience change.

approach.title: Design valid, efficient instruments

approach.title: Build a listening architecture
approach.body: We design an integrated listening architecture that combines an annual or semiannual census, targeted pulses, lifecycle surveys, open channels and periodic qualitative research. faqs.q: What is an employee listening strategy?
faqs.a: An employee listening strategy defines how an organization gathers, analyzes and acts on employee feedback across methods and moments. It usually combines periodic engagement surveys, short pulses, lifecycle surveys at events such as onboarding and exit, open feedback channels and qualitative research. A strong strategy specifies the purpose of each method, who owns it, how confidentiality is protected, and how results lead to visible action.

faqs.q: How often should we survey employees?
faqs.a: There is no single right frequency. Many organizations run a comprehensive survey once or twice a year, supplemented by short targeted pulses and lifecycle surveys. More frequent surveys only help if the organization can act on them; otherwise they create fatigue. We design cadence around decision cycles and capacity to respond, and we track participation and comment sentiment as signals of whether frequency is right.

faqs.q: How do you protect anonymity in employee surveys?

Open-text comments are reviewed for identifying details before broader sharing.

faqs.q: How do we analyze thousands of open-text comments?

This lets us quantify themes, compare them across groups and track them over time, while surfacing representative comments that illustrate each theme. Text analysis often reveals issues that closed-ended questions miss entirely.

faqs.q: What is data governance and why does it matter?

services.name: Pay Equity Analysis
services.meta_description: Pay equity analysis using regression-based models to find unexplained pay gaps by gender, race and ethnicity, with remediation plans and sound pay practices.
services.summary: Regression-based pay equity analysis that identifies unexplained gaps, guides fair remediation and strengthens the pay practices that created them.
services.lede: Our pay equity analysis uses regression-based statistical models to identify pay differences by gender, race and ethnicity that legitimate factors do not explain, then guides fair remediation and stronger pay practices going forward.
challenge: Pay equity has moved from a values question to a compliance and reputational priority. Pay transparency laws in a growing number of jurisdictions require salary ranges in job postings, and some require employers to report pay data by demographic group. Employees can now compare pay more easily than ever. At the same time, many organizations do not know whether they have unexplained pay gaps, or they rely on simple average comparisons that mix up differences in job, level and tenure with differences in treatment.

Pay gaps usually emerge from ordinary processes rather than deliberate decisions: starting salaries set by negotiation, inconsistent merit increases, off-cycle adjustments, acquisitions that brought different pay structures, and job architecture that leaves similar roles in different grades. Fixing individual salaries without addressing these root causes means gaps reappear. Effective pay equity analysis requires sound statistical methods, careful definition of comparable groups, attorney-client privilege where appropriate, defensible remediation, and changes to the pay practices themselves.

approach.title: Understand pay practices and context
approach.body: We interview compensation, HR and legal leaders to understand pay philosophy, job architecture, pay decision processes and recent organizational changes. We review policies for starting pay, merit, promotion and exceptions. Where appropriate, we listen to employee perceptions of pay fairness through focus groups or survey data, because perceived fairness matters alongside statistical findings.

approach.title: Build defensible statistical models
approach.body: We define similarly situated employee groupings, select legitimate pay factors such as job level, function, location, tenure and performance, and test them for potential bias. We use multiple regression to estimate pay differences by gender, race and ethnicity after controlling for those factors, and we flag statistically significant gaps and individual outliers. Cohort reviews complement regression where groups are too small for modeling.

approach.title: Design remediation and process fixes
approach.body: We model remediation scenarios, including the cost and effect of adjusting individuals below predicted pay, and help leaders choose an approach that is fair and defensible. We trace gaps to root causes and recommend process changes: structured starting pay guidelines, merit calibration, promotion pay rules, job architecture adjustments and controls on exceptions.

approach.title: Implement adjustments and communicate
approach.body: We support implementation of pay adjustments in coordination with payroll, legal counsel and managers. We help prepare communications for leaders, managers and employees, including guidance for managers on discussing pay. Where transparency or reporting requirements apply, we help prepare disclosures and pay range documentation consistent with your compensation structure.

approach.title: Monitor pay decisions continuously
approach.body: We build pay equity checks into compensation cycles so that new hires, promotions and merit increases are reviewed before decisions are final. We set up a recurring analysis cadence, typically annual, with dashboards for compensation teams and documented methodology for audit purposes. We train internal analysts to run models and interpret results consistently.

faqs.q: What is a pay equity analysis?
faqs.a: A pay equity analysis is a statistical review of whether employees doing comparable work are paid fairly, regardless of protected characteristics such as gender, race or ethnicity. It typically uses multiple regression to account for legitimate factors like job level, location and tenure, then tests whether any remaining pay differences are associated with demographic group. The analysis identifies gaps, individual outliers and the pay practices that contribute to them.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the pay gap and pay equity?
faqs.a: The raw pay gap compares average pay between groups across the whole organization, without accounting for differences in jobs or levels. It often reflects representation, such as fewer women in senior roles. Pay equity asks whether people in comparable roles with comparable qualifications are paid the same. Both matter: the adjusted gap reveals unequal treatment, while the raw gap points to opportunity and advancement issues.

faqs.q: Should pay equity analysis be conducted under attorney-client privilege?
faqs.a: Many organizations conduct the analysis at the direction of legal counsel to protect findings while they are reviewed and remediated. Whether privilege is appropriate depends on your legal context, jurisdiction and goals, including any public reporting commitments. We work with your internal or external counsel to structure the engagement appropriately and ensure that documentation supports both legal protection and practical action.

faqs.q: How often should we conduct a pay equity analysis?
faqs.a: We recommend a full analysis at least annually, ideally timed before the merit cycle so adjustments can be integrated into regular pay decisions. Organizations undergoing rapid growth, acquisitions or restructuring may need more frequent reviews. Building checks into hiring, promotion and merit processes provides continuous monitoring between full analyses and helps prevent new gaps from forming.

services.name: Equity Audits & DEI Analytics
services.meta_description: Equity audits and DEI analytics that examine hiring, promotion, performance and experience data to find where outcomes differ by group and what causes it.
services.summary: Rigorous review of hiring, advancement, performance, pay and experience data to find where outcomes differ across groups and which practices drive the differences.
services.lede: Our equity audit work examines hiring, promotion, performance, pay and employee experience data to identify where outcomes differ across groups and which policies and practices drive those differences, so leaders can act on evidence.
challenge: Organizations make commitments to fairness and inclusion, but many lack the evidence to know whether their practices produce equitable outcomes. Representation counts show who is in the organization, not why. Leaders cannot tell whether differences in promotion rates reflect qualifications, access to opportunity or bias in evaluation. Programs are launched without baselines and are hard to evaluate. Meanwhile the legal and political environment around diversity, equity and inclusion has become more complex, and leaders need approaches that are lawful, defensible and focused on fair processes for everyone.

An equity audit addresses these issues by examining the employee lifecycle as a system. Where in the hiring funnel do candidates from different groups drop out? Are performance ratings distributed differently, and do ratings predict outcomes equally well? Who gets stretch assignments, sponsorship and access to flexible work? Answering these questions requires careful statistics, sound handling of sensitive demographic data, qualitative insight into how processes actually work, and recommendations focused on practices and systems rather than on individuals.

approach.title: Understand processes and experiences
approach.body: We interview HR process owners, managers and employees across groups to understand how hiring, evaluation, promotion and assignment decisions are actually made. Focus groups and interviews surface experiences that data alone cannot show, such as informal sponsorship or access to information. We work with legal counsel to confirm the audit's scope and lawful use of demographic data.

approach.title: Analyze outcomes across the lifecycle
approach.body: We analyze adverse impact at each stage of the hiring funnel, promotion and exit rates, performance rating distributions, pay outcomes and survey results by demographic group, using appropriate statistical tests and controls. Intersectional analysis is applied where sample sizes allow. Where data is incomplete, we document limitations and recommend improvements to self-identification processes.

approach.title: Identify root causes and redesign practices
approach.body: We trace outcome differences to specific practices, such as unstructured interviews, vague performance criteria, informal promotion nominations or uneven access to development. We design improvements grounded in evidence: structured interviews and scoring rubrics, calibration protocols, transparent promotion criteria and fair allocation of opportunities. Redesigns are tested with managers and employees for practicality.

approach.title: Implement changes with managers
approach.body: We support implementation of redesigned processes, including manager training, updated guidance, and changes to HR systems and workflows. We help leaders communicate findings and actions appropriately to employees and boards. Changes are piloted where possible, with outcome measures defined in advance so leaders can see whether new practices are reducing unexplained differences.

approach.title: Monitor equity as an ongoing discipline
approach.body: We build equity measures into regular people reporting, with dashboards that track outcomes at each lifecycle stage while protecting small groups through minimum reporting thresholds. We establish governance for demographic data use, recurring audit cadence and accountability for process owners, so that equity becomes part of routine management rather than a periodic initiative.

Clients engage us when they need a baseline before setting goals, after employee concerns or a legal claim, when existing programs have not shifted outcomes, ahead of investor or regulatory disclosure, or when they want to refocus DEI work on fair processes and measurable results. For customers and communities, organizations whose workforce reflects and understands them are often better able to serve them well.

faqs.q: What is an equity audit?
faqs.a: An equity audit is a systematic review of an organization's people data, policies and practices to determine whether outcomes such as hiring, promotion, pay, performance ratings and retention differ across demographic groups, and why. It combines statistical analysis with interviews and process review to identify root causes. The goal is to find and fix practices that produce unfair outcomes, using evidence rather than assumptions.

faqs.q: What is adverse impact analysis?
faqs.a: Adverse impact analysis tests whether a selection process, such as a hiring screen or promotion decision, results in substantially different selection rates for different groups. Common approaches include the four-fifths rule of thumb and statistical significance tests. Adverse impact does not on its own prove discrimination, but it signals that a practice deserves closer examination to confirm it is job-related and to consider fairer alternatives.

faqs.q: How do you handle demographic data responsibly?
faqs.a: We use demographic data only for defined purposes such as auditing fairness, with access restricted to a small analytics team. We apply minimum group sizes in reporting to avoid identifying individuals and suppress small intersectional cells. We work with legal counsel on lawful use in each jurisdiction and recommend voluntary, well-explained self-identification processes so employees understand why data is collected and how it is protected.

faqs.q: Is an equity audit the same as a DEI program?
faqs.a: No. An equity audit is a diagnostic. It examines whether existing processes produce fair outcomes and identifies what to change. DEI programs are interventions, such as training, mentoring or employee groups. An audit helps leaders decide which interventions are warranted and evaluate whether existing ones are working. Many of the most effective changes it identifies involve redesigning core talent processes rather than adding new programs.

services.name: Predictive Retention Analytics
services.meta_description: Predictive retention analytics using survival analysis and fair models to explain why employees leave, find rising risk early and target retention well.
services.summary: Attrition modeling with survival analysis and fairness testing that shows who is likely to leave, when, and why, so retention efforts reach the right people.
services.lede: Our employee retention analytics use survival analysis and carefully governed predictive models to explain why people leave, identify rising attrition risk early, and help managers act on the factors they can actually influence.
challenge: Turnover is one of the most expensive and disruptive people problems an organization faces. Each departure carries recruiting and training costs, lost productivity, knowledge loss and strain on remaining colleagues, and in customer-facing roles it erodes service quality and relationships. Yet most organizations respond to attrition after the fact. Exit interviews arrive too late, are often candid only in part, and are rarely analyzed systematically. Monthly turnover reports show what happened but not why, or who is likely to leave next.

Predictive models can help, but they also carry risks. A model that flags individuals as flight risks without explanation can lead to unfair treatment, damage trust, or encode historical bias. Simple models built on annual turnover rates ignore timing: an employee who leaves at three months differs from one who leaves at five years. Effective employee retention analytics use methods suited to time-to-event data, explain the drivers in actionable terms, are tested for fairness, and are embedded in clear governance about how predictions can be used.

approach.title: Learn why people stay and leave
approach.body: We analyze exit interview and survey comments, and conduct stay interviews and focus groups with current employees, including recently hired and long-tenured staff. We talk with managers about what they observe before people leave. This qualitative evidence generates hypotheses about drivers, such as scheduling, manager relationships, pay competitiveness or career paths, and informs which data to include in models.

approach.title: Model attrition with survival analysis
approach.body: We assemble data on tenure, role, pay position, manager, performance, schedule, commute, mobility and engagement. Using survival analysis, including Kaplan-Meier curves and Cox proportional hazards models, we estimate how risk changes over tenure and which factors accelerate or delay departure. Where useful we add machine learning models, validated on holdout data and tested for disparate impact across demographic groups.

approach.title: Design targeted retention interventions
approach.body: We translate drivers into interventions aimed at the factors the organization controls: onboarding improvements for early-tenure risk, pay adjustments where market position drives exits, scheduling changes, manager coaching or clearer career paths. We size the expected effect of each option and design pilots with control groups where feasible, so leaders can learn what actually reduces attrition.

approach.title: Equip managers and HR to act
approach.body: We deliver risk insights to HR business partners and managers through team-level views that focus on drivers and recommended actions, typically not individual scores. We train managers in stay conversations and support HR in running retention pilots. Communication with employees about how data is used helps maintain trust.

approach.title: Govern, monitor and refresh models
approach.body: We establish model governance covering permitted uses, access, fairness testing, documentation and periodic validation. We monitor model performance and drift, refresh models as conditions change, and track whether interventions are reducing regretted attrition. Internal analysts receive documented code and training so they can maintain the models responsibly.

services.who_we_serve: Chief people officers, HR business partners, people analytics leaders, chief operating officers and private equity operating partners. Common triggers include rising or persistently high turnover in critical or frontline roles, early-tenure attrition, retention risk during an acquisition or restructuring, staffing shortages affecting service or safety, or a desire to quantify the cost of turnover. We work with health systems, hospitality and retail operators, technology firms, financial services companies, manufacturers and portfolio companies.
services.impact_lens: Reducing avoidable turnover benefits employees first: it usually means better onboarding, fairer pay, more humane schedules, stronger managers and clearer paths to grow. Stable teams provide more consistent care and service to customers, patients and students. Lower churn reduces the burden on colleagues who cover vacancies. For communities, steadier employment supports household stability. Careful governance ensures predictive tools help employees rather than label them, preserving trust in how the organization uses people data.

faqs.q: Can you really predict which employees will leave?
faqs.a: Models can estimate the relative likelihood of departure for groups and individuals with useful accuracy, but no model predicts individual decisions with certainty. People leave for personal reasons that data cannot see. The greatest value usually comes not from individual predictions but from understanding the drivers and timing of attrition, which lets organizations address root causes. We use predictions carefully and within clear governance.

faqs.q: Why use survival analysis for attrition?
faqs.a: Survival analysis is designed for time-to-event data, so it models not just whether someone leaves but when. It handles employees who have not yet left, known as censored observations, correctly, which simpler methods do not. It shows how risk changes over tenure, such as spikes at the first anniversary, and estimates how factors like pay position or schedule shift that risk over time.

faqs.q: Should managers see individual flight-risk scores?
faqs.a: In most cases we recommend against it. Individual scores can lead to unfair treatment, self-fulfilling outcomes or privacy concerns. We typically provide managers with team-level insights about risk drivers and suggested actions, such as holding stay conversations or addressing scheduling issues. Individual-level use, where appropriate, should be limited to HR professionals with clear guidelines and a focus on support.

faqs.q: How do you make sure a retention model is fair?
faqs.a: We test model predictions and errors across demographic groups to check whether some groups are flagged more often or predicted less accurately. We review input variables for proxies of protected characteristics, document model design and limitations, and establish rules for how predictions can be used. Fairness testing is repeated whenever the model is refreshed, as part of ongoing model governance.

services.name: Impact & People Dashboards
services.meta_title: Impact & People Dashboards: Design and Build
services.meta_description: People dashboards and impact dashboards designed around real decisions, with clear metrics, privacy safeguards and governance so leaders use them well.
services.summary: Decision-focused dashboards for workforce, experience and social impact measures, with sound metric definitions, privacy safeguards and governance that keep them trusted.
services.lede: We design and build people dashboards and impact dashboards around the decisions executives, boards, funders and managers actually make, with clear metric definitions, privacy safeguards and governance that keep the numbers trusted and used.
challenge: Dashboards are easy to build and hard to make useful. Many organizations have dozens of reports that are rarely opened, show too many metrics without context, and answer questions nobody asked. Leaders still request one-off analyses because existing dashboards do not reflect the decisions in front of them. Metrics such as turnover, engagement or people served are defined differently across systems, so numbers do not reconcile and confidence erodes. Boards and investors receive human capital data in inconsistent formats from one quarter to the next.

Impact reporting presents an additional challenge. Mission-driven organizations, impact investors and companies with social commitments need to show outcomes for people and communities, not just activity counts. That requires a clear theory of change, outcome indicators, and data that may come from surveys, program records or partners. People data also brings privacy risk: dashboards that slice results too finely can expose individuals. Well-designed people dashboards are built around decisions, use a limited set of meaningful indicators, protect privacy, and include a plan for who acts on what.

approach.title: Start with users and decisions
approach.body: We interview dashboard users, from board members and executives to HR partners, program managers and frontline supervisors, to understand the decisions they make, how often, and what information would change them. We review existing reports and how they are used. Users help define what a useful dashboard looks like before any design begins.

approach.title: Define indicators that mean something
approach.body: We select a focused set of leading and lagging indicators linked to strategy or theory of change, and write precise metric definitions with formulas, sources, refresh frequency and owners. For impact dashboards, we align indicators with recognized frameworks where relevant. We assess data quality for each indicator and resolve inconsistencies across systems before anything is visualized.

approach.title: Design for clarity and privacy
approach.body: We design dashboards that answer questions in order of importance, with context such as targets, trends and comparisons, and with accessible visual design that meets WCAG contrast and screen reader needs. We apply minimum group sizes and role-based views to protect privacy. Prototypes are tested with users and refined until the key message is clear at a glance.

approach.title: Build, integrate and launch
approach.body: We build dashboards in your chosen business intelligence platform or recommend one if needed, with automated data pipelines where feasible. We document data lineage and calculations, test accuracy against source systems, and train users to interpret the information and to recognize its limits. Launches include working sessions that connect dashboards to real decisions and meeting rhythms.

approach.title: Govern metrics and keep them relevant
approach.body: We establish metric ownership, a data dictionary, change control for definitions, and a periodic review to retire unused views and add new questions. We monitor usage to see which dashboards inform decisions. Internal teams receive documentation and training to maintain dashboards, and we help design board and investor reporting packages that stay consistent over time.

services.impact_lens: Dashboards shape attention, and attention shapes action. When organizations track employee wellbeing, fairness and development alongside financial results, those outcomes receive the management focus they deserve. faqs.q: What should a people dashboard include?
faqs.a: A people dashboard should include a focused set of indicators tied to strategic priorities, typically covering workforce composition, hiring, retention, internal mobility, engagement or experience, and fairness measures such as pay equity or promotion rates. It should combine leading indicators, which signal future outcomes, with lagging indicators that confirm results. Each metric needs a clear definition, a target or benchmark for context, and an owner responsible for action.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a people dashboard and an impact dashboard?
faqs.a: A people dashboard focuses on the workforce: talent, experience, fairness and capability. An impact dashboard tracks outcomes for the people and communities an organization serves, such as program reach, client outcomes or social and environmental results, usually guided by a theory of change. Many mission-driven organizations and impact investors benefit from both, viewed together, because workforce health often shapes the quality of impact.

faqs.q: Which dashboard tools do you work with?
faqs.a: We work with common business intelligence platforms as well as the reporting modules within HR and program management systems. We are not tied to any vendor. Where clients do not yet have a platform, we help assess options based on existing technology, budget, data sources, security requirements and internal skills, and we design dashboards so that definitions and logic are documented independently of the tool.

faqs.q: How do you keep people dashboards from exposing individuals?
faqs.a: We apply minimum group sizes so that results for small teams or demographic groups are suppressed, use role-based access so users see only what their role requires, and avoid filters that allow combinations to isolate individuals. Sensitive measures such as pay or demographic data receive additional controls. These safeguards are documented in governance policies and tested before launch.
